findings.summary: The second mandatory regression is sequential, not concurrent: the governed-writer process is joined via communicate() and has fully released the lock before source.adopt() is called, so adoption never contends. Consequently neither mandatory test fails against an adopt() that performs its byte CAS before acquiring the lock and then writes/commits without re-reading (test 1 passes because the bytes are valid throughout the hold window; test 2 passes because the pre-lock read already observes the winner's bytes). That defeats the spec's Done criterion that the tests 'would fail if adopt() ... trusted a pre-lock CAS' and leaves the test's own 'adoption must re-read under lock' requirement unproven. The arrangement needs adoption to start and read before the winner commits (e.g. writer acquires and holds, adoption blocks on the lock, writer then commits the competing state and releases).

_adopt_under_lock stages with an explicit pathspec but commits the whole index, so any pre-existing staged entry outside the confirmed logical filenames would be swept into the adoption commit. The new lock removes the normal interleaving that could cause this, so it is a residual (pre-existing) hazard only after a crashed prior transaction; a pathspec commit or an index-cleanliness precheck would close it against the spec's 'only the confirmed logical filenames may be staged and committed'.
